rows.en: My name's Tom.
Nice to meet you!
And what's your name?
What's your name? · formal, with Lei
What's your name? · informal, with a friend

cards.headline: When someone asks how you are

rows.en: How are you?
I'm well, thanks.
And you?
How are you? · formal
How are you? · informal
And you? · formal
And you? · informal

cards.headline: Asking after someone: Lei or tu

rows.en: How are you? · formal
How are you? · informal
And you? · formal
And you? · informal
Good morning!
Good evening, ma'am.
Buonanotte is for when someone is going to bed.
Good night, see you tomorrow!

cards.headline: When evening starts
cards.note: Buonasera starts surprisingly early, around 3 or 4 p.m. From then on it's the greeting for the rest of the day, even at 9 p.m. Buongiorno covers the morning and early afternoon.

rows.en: Sorry, I didn't understand.
Could you repeat that, please?

rows.text: Può ripetere più piano, per favore?
rows.en: Could you say that again more slowly, please?

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Asking someone to speak more slowly, with più piano, per favore, is perfectly normal here. Most people are pleased that you're trying to speak Italian.

cards.headline: When someone asks where you're from

rows.en: Where are you from?
I'm American.
I'm American (a woman says this).

cards.headline: When you say where you live

rows.en: Are you here on vacation?
No, I live here.
Where you live starts with abito.

cards.headline: When you say how long you've been here

rows.en: How long have you lived here?
I've lived here for a month.
Italian uses the present: the time is still going.

rows.text: Da quanto tempo è in Italia?
rows.en: How long have you been in Italy? · formal

rows.text: Da quanto tempo sei in Italia?
rows.en: How long have you been in Italy? · informal
Did you get that?
Yes, got it, thanks!
Ho capito means you got it, about something just said.
Did you get that? · formal
Did you get that? · informal, with a friend
Yes, got it.

cards.headline: When you hear a word you don't know

rows.en: Sorry, what does “scontrino” mean?
“Scontrino” means “receipt.”
Use cosa vuol dire for a word you heard.

cards.headline: When you need a word in Italian

rows.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?
You say “scontrino.”
Use come si dice for a word you need.

cards.headline: When you ask the price of one thing

rows.en: How much is the newspaper?
It's two euros.
How much is the newspaper?
How much are the peaches?
They're three euros.
Good morning! What are you having?
I'd like a cappuccino, please.
I'll have a sparkling water, thanks.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Cappuccino is a morning drink. After lunch, Italians order an espresso instead.

cards.headline: When you order one or two

rows.en: A cappuccino, please.
Two croissants, please.

rows.text: Una spremuta e due caffè, per favore.
rows.en: A fresh juice and two espressos, please.
two cappuccinos · -o becomes -i
two fresh juices · -a becomes -e
two espressos · stays the same

rows.text: Quanto costano un caffè e un cornetto?
rows.en: How much for an espresso and a croissant?
Two euros seventy.
A price is the euros, then e and the cents. Euro stays the same.
Before uno and otto the tens lose their last letter.
That's twenty-eight euros.
That's thirty-one euros.

cards.headline: When you have to do something at an office

rows.en: You have to take a ticket.
Do you have to book the appointment online?
Bisogna is followed by a verb and never changes.

cards.headline: When you need one thing or more

rows.text: Serve una marca da bollo da sedici euro.
rows.en: You need a sixteen-euro revenue stamp.
You need two passport photos.
Use serve for one thing, servono for more than one.

cards.headline: When you want to pay by card

rows.en: Can I pay by card?

rows.text: Sì, certo, può pagare anche con la carta.
rows.en: Yes, of course, you can pay by card too.
Posso pagare asks if you can pay. Then add how: con la carta.

cards.headline: When you want to pay cash

rows.en: Can I pay cash?

rows.text: Certo, può pagare in contanti, nessun problema.
rows.en: Sure, you can pay cash, no problem.
Small shops and market stalls often prefer cash for small amounts.

rows.text: Per il contratto basta la fotocopia?
rows.en: For the lease, is a photocopy enough?
Yes, a photocopy is enough.

rows.text: E di fototessere ne bastano due.
rows.en: And two passport photos are enough.

cards.headline: When you ask how long it takes

rows.en: How long does it take?
It takes a few weeks.
Ci vuole goes with one thing; ci vogliono with several.

cards.headline: When a clerk gives you instructions

rows.en: Fill out the form.
Sign here at the bottom.

rows.text: Torni con la ricevuta fra trenta giorni.
rows.en: Come back with the receipt in thirty days.
Sign here at the bottom.
Take a ticket and wait.
-are verbs end in -i; -ere and -ire in -a.
Che links a thing to what you say about it.
Italian always says che, even where English drops "that."

rows.text: Il conto che ho aperto è gratuito.
rows.en: The account I opened is free.

rows.text: L'idraulico che chiamo di solito è in ferie.
rows.en: The plumber I usually call is on vacation.

rows.text: Allora, prendi il bilocale che abbiamo visto ieri?
rows.en: So, are you taking the one-bedroom we saw yesterday?

cards.headline: Learn it

rows.text: Non capisco bene quello che c'è scritto qui.
rows.en: I don't really understand what it says here.

rows.text: Mi dica pure quello che non è chiaro.
rows.en: Just tell me what isn't clear.
It's just what I was looking for.

cards.note: Quello che means "the thing that." It's how Italian says "what" in these sentences.

rows.text: Quello che conta è la firma.
rows.en: What matters is the signature. · everyday

rows.text: Ciò che conta è la firma.
rows.en: What matters is the signature. · more formal
Come mai asks how come: why something is so.
Why Italy, of all places?

rows.text: Come mai? L'ho consegnato a maggio!
rows.en: How come? I turned it in in May!

cards.headline: When you ask how long or how much

rows.en: How long is the course?

rows.text: Quanto costa il corso al mese?
rows.en: How much is the course per month?
Quanto asks both how long and how much.
This one's brighter than the other one.

rows.text: Il treno è più veloce del pullman.
rows.en: The train is faster than the bus.
Più plus di compares two things.

rows.text: È l'albergo più tranquillo della zona.
rows.en: It's the quietest hotel in the area.

rows.text: Allora secondo me è il migliore.
rows.en: Then I think it's the best one.
Il or la before più picks the top one; il migliore means "the best."
Put con, di or in first, then cui.

rows.text: La persona con cui ho parlato ieri oggi non c'è.
rows.en: The person I talked to yesterday isn't here today.

rows.text: Ecco, è questo il documento di cui ho bisogno.
rows.en: There, this is the document I need.
For a place, in cui and dove mean the same.

rows.text: In quale filiale ritiri la carta?
rows.en: Which branch do you pick up your card at?

rows.text: In quella in cui ho aperto il conto.
rows.en: At the one where I opened my account.

rows.text: In quella dove ho aperto il conto.
rows.en: At the one where I opened my account.
Excuse me, is it okay to go in?
Can you take photos?

rows.text: Sì, ma non si può usare il flash.
rows.en: Yes, but you can't use the flash.
Can you use the flash?
Can you take photos?
A plural like foto takes si possono.

cards.headline: Saying how long you've lived somewhere

rows.text: Da quanto tempo vivi in questa città?
rows.en: How long have you lived in this city?
I've been living here for two years.

rows.text: Sono due anni che vivo qui.
rows.en: I've been living here for two years.

cards.headline: Sono … che, or è for one

rows.text: Sono già due settimane che aspetto l'idraulico.
rows.en: I've been waiting for the plumber for two weeks already.
With one week or one month, it's è.

rows.text: È un mese che il citofono non funziona.
rows.en: The buzzer hasn't worked in a month.

cards.headline: When you want a little more

rows.text: Me ne dà un pezzetto da assaggiare?
rows.en: Could I have a little piece to taste?
Do you like it? Would you like some more?

rows.text: È buonissimo. Me ne dà ancora un etto?
rows.en: It's delicious. Could I have another hundred grams?
Ne means "of it" or "of them".
I'll bring you two.

rows.text: Me ne dà ancora due fette?
rows.en: Could I have two more slices?
With an amount, ne is always there.
Glielo means it to him, to her or to you. The context tells you which.
I'll tell him myself.
If you like, I'll bring it to you tonight.
I'm happy to lend it to you.
I can order it for you.
Same thing: glielo goes before posso.
I can read it to you, if you'd like.
Sorry, I forgot all about it!

rows.text: Il pane? Me ne sono dimenticata anch'io.
rows.en: The bread? I forgot about it too.

rows.text: La bolletta? Me ne dimentico sempre.
rows.en: The bill? I always forget about it.
Ne goes before the verb: me ne, te ne, se ne.
Did you remember?
Sorry, I forgot all about it!
No, he forgot all about it.

cards.headline: Saying "it to me" and "it to you"

rows.en: Could you wrap it for me, please?

rows.text: La torta? Te la porto stasera.
rows.en: The cake? I'll bring it over tonight.

rows.text: Le chiavi? Te le restituisco stasera.
rows.en: The keys? I'll give them back to you tonight.
Me or te comes first, then lo, la, li or le to match the thing.
Could you wrap it for me, please?
It's a gift.
In almost any shop, they'll gift-wrap it for free.

cards.headline: When someone asks to come in

rows.en: May I come in?
Please, come on in!
Please, sit down.
After the verb, pure means "go ahead," not "also."
Come on in!
Go ahead and give me your bag.
Take your time.

cards.headline: Telling someone to do it, or not to

rows.text: Prenda il primo autobus che passa.
rows.en: Take the first bus that comes.

rows.text: Non prenda il 40, oggi non passa.
rows.en: Don't take the 40, it's not running today.
Put non in front to say don't.

rows.text: Non si preoccupi, Le tengo io il posto.
rows.en: Don't worry, I'll save your seat.
Verbs in -are take -i.

rows.text: Giri alla prima a destra, per favore.
rows.en: Take the first right, please.
Other verbs take -a.

rows.text: Prenda il primo autobus che passa.
rows.en: Take the first bus that comes.
Andare becomes vada.

rows.text: Vada sempre dritto, poi giri a destra.
rows.en: Go straight ahead, then turn right.

cards.headline: When you say what you do

rows.en: What do you do for a living?
I work as a teacher.
What field are you in?
I work in marketing.
Please wait a few minutes.
Is there a problem?
Qualche always takes a singular noun: qualche minuto.
Would you like something hot?
I'd like something hot.
With a describing word, it means something of that kind.
First the scene, then what happened.

rows.text: Stavo cucinando quando è saltata la luce.
rows.en: I was cooking when the power went out.

rows.text: Leggevo a letto quando è suonato il telefono.
rows.en: I was reading in bed when the phone rang.

rows.text: Pioveva forte quando siamo usciti dal museo.
rows.en: It was pouring when we came out of the museum.

cards.headline: Two ways to say nobody did it

rows.en: Nobody helped us.
Nobody helped us.
Same meaning; after the verb, add non before it.
There was nobody at the front desk.

rows.text: E poi non è venuto nessuno?
rows.en: And then nobody came?
No, nobody came.

rows.text: Siccome pioveva, abbiamo preso un taxi.
rows.en: Since it was raining, we took a taxi.

rows.text: Abbiamo preso un taxi perché pioveva.
rows.en: We took a taxi because it was raining.
Siccome puts the reason first; perché puts it after.

rows.text: Ormai era tardi, quindi ho cenato con pane e formaggio.
rows.en: Too late by then, so I had bread and cheese.

rows.text: C'era sciopero, quindi ho preso il pullman.
rows.en: There was a strike, so I took the bus.
Quindi brings in the result.

cards.headline: When one thing happened before another

rows.text: Quando siamo arrivati, il treno era già partito.
rows.en: When we got there, the train had already left.

rows.text: Quando è saltata la luce, avevo già cenato.
rows.en: When the power went out, I'd already had dinner.

rows.text: Avevo lasciato gli occhiali sul tavolo.
rows.en: I'd left my glasses on the table.

cards.headline: When you say you'd never done something

rows.text: Non avevo mai visto tanta gente.
rows.en: I'd never seen so many people.

rows.text: Non avevo mai mangiato una pizza così buona.
rows.en: I'd never had such good pizza.
Non avevo mai + past participle: you'd never done it before.

cards.headline: When someone asks if you can make it

rows.text: Ce la fai per le otto?
rows.en: Can you make it by eight?
Yes, I can make it.
Ce la fai? asks if you can manage it.

cards.headline: The little words change with the person

rows.en: I can make it
you can make it
I'm getting by
you're getting by

cards.headline: Two pasts for the same story

rows.en: The merchant died without children. · in stories

rows.text: Il mercante è morto senza figli.
rows.en: The merchant died without children. · everyday
Same meaning; you only need to recognize the first.

cards.headline: When you say it another way

rows.text: Cioè, voglio dire che è stancante.
rows.en: I mean, what I'm saying is it's tiring.
What do you mean? Can you explain?

rows.text: Mi spiego meglio: sono quattro ore di fila.
rows.en: Let me put it another way: four hours straight.

cards.headline: When you ask who made it

rows.text: Scusi, quando è stata costruita questa chiesa?
rows.en: Excuse me, when was this church built?

rows.text: E questo affresco, da chi è stato dipinto?
rows.en: And who painted this fresco?

rows.text: È stato dipinto da un allievo di Giotto.
rows.en: It was painted by one of Giotto's pupils.
The verb matches the thing (stata, stato); the maker comes after da.

rows.text: Prima di firmare, vorrei leggere le condizioni.
rows.en: Before I sign, I'd like to read the terms.

rows.text: Prima che tu parta, ti do il mio numero.
rows.en: Before you leave, I'll give you my number.

rows.text: Te la riporto prima che faccia buio.
rows.en: I'll bring it back before it gets dark.
Same person: prima di. Someone else or weather: prima che.
I know it's closed.

rows.text: È vero che qui la gente cena tardi.
rows.en: It's true people eat late here.

rows.text: Secondo me è un po' caro.
rows.en: If you ask me, it's a little expensive.
The verb stays as usual after each one.

rows.text: Penso che il museo sia chiuso.
rows.en: I think the museum's closed.
I hope Marco comes too.
I think they're right.
After penso che, the verb changes: sia, venga, abbia.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many museums and shops close one day a week, so you'll often be guessing whether a place is open. Penso che sia chiuso is a phrase you'll use a lot.

cards.headline: When you give a friend advice

rows.text: È meglio che tu non beva caffè la sera.
rows.en: It's better if you don't drink coffee in the evening.

rows.text: Se fossi in te, studierei di più.
rows.en: If I were you, I'd study more.

rows.text: Se fossi in te, chiederei alla padrona di casa.
rows.en: If I were you, I'd ask the landlady.
It means 'if I were you' and never changes.

rows.text: Se fossi in te, non berrei caffè la sera.
rows.en: If I were you, I wouldn't drink coffee in the evening.

rows.text: Se fossi in te, cercherei un'altra casa.
rows.en: If I were you, I'd look for another place.
Agree to something, on one condition: as long as.

rows.text: Te la presto, purché tu la chiuda col lucchetto.
rows.en: I'll lend it, as long as you lock it up.

rows.text: Va bene, purché tu faccia il pieno.
rows.en: Okay, as long as you fill the tank.
Unless something happens: it names what would stop the plan.

rows.text: A meno che non piova, domani andiamo al mare.
rows.en: Unless it rains, we'll go to the beach tomorrow.

rows.text: Sì, a meno che non faccia troppo freddo.
rows.en: Yes, unless it's too cold.

cards.headline: When you hope something went well

rows.text: Spero che tu abbia dormito bene.
rows.en: I hope you slept well.

rows.text: Spero che il colloquio sia andato bene!
rows.en: I hope the interview went well!

cards.headline: When you think something has already happened

rows.en: I think she's already here.
I don't think they understood.

rows.text: Penso che Anna sia arrivata ieri.
rows.en: I think Anna got here yesterday.

rows.text: Sono contenta che tu sia qui.
rows.en: I'm glad you're here.
I'm so glad to see you!
Someone else: che + subjunctive. Yourself: di + verb.

rows.text: Mi dispiace molto che stia male.
rows.en: I'm so sorry he's not well.

rows.text: Mi dispiace di non poter venire.
rows.en: I'm sorry I can't come.
Someone else: che + subjunctive. Yourself: di + verb.
What great news!
What a shame!
How lucky!
Che plus noun makes an exclamation, without “a”.
What a great opportunity!
What bad luck!
What a deal!

rows.text: In bocca al lupo per il colloquio!
rows.en: Good luck with the interview!
Thanks!
Say it before any exam or interview.
Best wishes!
Thanks!
Used for birthdays, weddings, births and holidays.
Say what you'd like someone else to do. The verb takes the -ssi form.

rows.text: Vorrei che mi chiamassi quando arrivi.
rows.en: I'd like you to call me when you get there.

rows.text: Vorrei che mi parlassi in italiano.
rows.en: I'd like you to talk to me in Italian.

rows.text: Che peccato, vorrei che ci fossi anche tu.
rows.en: That's too bad, I wish you could be there too.
Alone, it answers a hope. With -ssi, it's a wish.
If only! But I have to work.
If only we actually won!
If only I had more time!
If it rains, I'll stay home. · likely
If it rained, I'd stay home. · only imagined
Se plus the present: it may well happen.

cards.headline: When you imagine what you'd do

rows.text: Cosa faresti se vincessi alla lotteria?
rows.en: What would you do if you won the lottery?

rows.text: Se vincessi, comprerei una casa in campagna.
rows.en: If I won, I'd buy a house in the country.
Se plus the -ssi form, then the 'would' form. Hold the double s.
Soul and body.
Wholeheartedly, totally.

rows.text: Si è dedicato al progetto anima e corpo.
rows.en: He threw himself into the project wholeheartedly.
Climbing up mirrors.
Clutching at straws with flimsy excuses.
Stop clutching at straws!
To have your heart in your throat.
Your heart is pounding, from fear or nerves.

rows.text: Prima dell'esame avevo il cuore in gola.
rows.en: Before the exam my heart was pounding.
Having the jack (bowls) of something.
To have a fixed idea or obsession.

rows.text: Marco ha il pallino della fotografia.
rows.en: Marco is obsessed with photography.
To have the moon crooked.
To be in a bad mood.

rows.text: Oggi ho la luna storta, scusami.
rows.en: I'm in a bad mood today, sorry.
Have Job's patience.
Have endless patience.

rows.text: Con tre figli ha la pazienza di Giobbe.
rows.en: With three kids, she has endless patience.
To have goose skin.
To have goosebumps, from cold or emotion.

rows.text: Questa canzone mi fa venire la pelle d'oca.
rows.en: This song gives me goosebumps.

cards.headline: A saying

rows.text: Avere la testa fra le nuvole.
rows.en: To have your head in the clouds.
To be absent-minded.

rows.text: Scusa, avevo la testa fra le nuvole.
rows.en: Sorry, I had my head in the clouds.

keys: idiom:avere la testa fra le nuvole

rows.en: To have holed hands.
To spend money too easily.

To have your hands tied.
To be unable to act.

rows.text: Vorrei aiutarti, ma ho le mani legate.

To be rotten wrong.
To be completely wrong.
You're completely wrong about this.
To have a devil for every hair.
To be fuming, in a foul temper.

rows.en: My sister is fuming.
Literally: to give out numbers
To talk nonsense, to lose it; a machine acting up.

Literally: to go rolling
To go to ruin, to fall apart.

rows.text: Senza di te tutto va a rotoli.
rows.en: Without you everything falls apart.
Literally: to go up in smoke
To come to nothing: money, plans, work.

rows.text: Tutti i nostri progetti sono andati in fumo.
rows.en: All our plans came to nothing.
Literally: to sew on a button
To strike up a conversation, often with a stranger.

rows.text: Ha attaccato bottone con me sul treno.
rows.en: He struck up a conversation with me on the train.
Literally: to have a tail of straw

rows.text: Ha la coda di paglia, si offende per tutto.

Literally: to have a nail fixed in

Literally: to drop like a bean

Another meeting? What a drag!

To cost a fortune.

In an instant.
I'll be there in an instant.
The habit doesn't make the monk.
Don't judge by appearances.

rows.text: Sembra severo, ma l'abito non fa il monaco.

cards.headline: A saying

rows.text: non avere né capo né coda

It makes no sense.

rows.en: to be left with empty hands
To come away with nothing.

cards.headline: A saying

rows.en: to break the boxes (a polite stand-in)

rows.text: Ho cambiato lavoro, ma è peggio: dalla padella alla brace!

it doesn't rain on that
No doubt about it.

rows.text: È il migliore, su questo non ci piove.
rows.en: He's the best, no doubt about it.
for a good understander, few words
A word to the wise is enough.

rows.text: Non dico altro: a buon intenditor poche parole.
rows.en: I'll say no more: a word to the wise.
at every death of a pope
Very rarely; once in a blue moon.

rows.text: Ci vediamo a ogni morte di papa.
rows.en: We see each other once in a blue moon.
in instalments
In episodes, bit by bit.

rows.text: Mi ha raccontato tutto a puntate.
rows.en: He told me everything bit by bit.
water in your mouth!
Keep it quiet; mum's the word.

rows.text: È una sorpresa, quindi acqua in bocca!
rows.en: It's a surprise, so mum's the word!
on the day's agenda
Happening all the time; routine.

rows.text: Qui i ritardi sono all'ordine del giorno.
rows.en: Here delays happen all the time.
in the light of the sun

rows.text: Ha fatto tutto alla luce del sole.
rows.en: He did everything in the open.
to raise your elbow
To drink too much.

rows.text: Alla festa ha alzato un po' il gomito.

cards.headline: About this pharmacy
cards.note: Prati means meadows. Once flood-prone land by the Tiber, it was laid out on a regular grid from the 1880s for officials of the new capital, so it feels unlike the winding old centre.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The ceiling of Il Gesù, finished in 1679, shows painted figures tumbling out of their frame. Stucco figures are mixed in with the painted ones, so the eye cannot tell where one ends and the other begins.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Rome has two big football clubs, Lazio and Roma, and both play at the Stadio Olimpico, so the same stands fill with different fans every other week. Their match, the Derby della Capitale, often splits families.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Testaccio grew up around Rome's slaughterhouse. Workers were often paid partly in leftovers: tripe, tail, offal. Called the quinto quarto, the fifth quarter, they became dishes like coda alla vaccinara that local families still cook and argue over.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Peperoni cruschi are sweet red peppers dried in the sun, a way to keep them through the winter when fresh food was scarce. Just before eating, they're fried for seconds in hot oil until they crisp and crackle.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Once called a national shame, the Sassi were emptied in the 1950s. Today they are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Older people still remember the shame; the young are proud of the change.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Matera people give the cucù, a small hand-painted terracotta rooster whistle, as a gift for good luck and good wishes. It's given at weddings or when someone starts a new life. You blow into the tail.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every 2 July, a huge papier-mâché cart for the patron saint is paraded through town. At the square, the crowd rushes in and tears it apart, and everyone wants a piece for good luck.

cards.headline: About this street-food stall
cards.note: Lampredotto is the fourth stomach of the cow, simmered for hours in broth. It was working people's food, sold from street carts by the trippai, who used the cheaper cuts nobody else wanted.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Every June, sand is spread over the piazza for the Calcio Storico, an old, rough ball game. Four teams play, one for each historic quarter of the city.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Fiorentina fans wear purple, called viola, and no rival is more disliked than Juventus. When star player Roberto Baggio was sold to Juventus in 1990, fans rioted in the streets.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Santo Spirito's facade was never decorated, so it still stands smooth and pale above the square. Brunelleschi designed the church but died in 1446, before it was built, and the work carried on without him.

cards.headline: About this shop
cards.note: The prize of the Palio is not money but the drappellone, a large banner painted anew for every race. An artist is chosen each time, so no two are alike. The winning contrada keeps it in its museum.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Palazzo Salimbeni is the seat of Monte dei Paschi di Siena, one of the oldest banks in the world still operating. It began in 1472 as a public fund lending to the poor at fair terms.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Sarde in saor, fried sardines in a sweet-and-sour mix of onions, vinegar, raisins and pine nuts, began as a way to keep fish for days. It tastes better the day after, so good cooks make it ahead.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: One statue in Campo dei Mori, Sior Rioba, is traditionally said to have an iron nose, replacing a stone one he lost. The figures are said to show merchants from the Morea, in Greece.

cards.headline: About this gondola workshop
cards.note: The hull of a gondola is deliberately asymmetrical, wider on the left. That way a gondolier rowing from one side can still move in a straight line.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: When something good happens, a Neapolitan may pay for two coffees and drink one. The second is a caffè sospeso, left at the bar for the next person who can't afford it. Nobody asks who takes it.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: In Piazza Bellini you can still see stretches of Naples' original Greek walls, made of big tuff blocks, a few metres below street level. Students now sit at café tables over a wall more than 2,000 years old.

cards.headline: About this bakery
cards.note: The sfogliatella comes in two kinds, and every Neapolitan has a favourite. The riccia has many thin crisp layers shaped like a shell. The frolla is rounder and softer, made of shortcrust pastry.

cards.headline: About this pizzeria
cards.note: In Naples the pizza is soft and elastic, and the edge puffs up in the very hot oven. That raised edge is the sign of a well-made dough that has risen slowly.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Bologna, ragù is served with tagliatelle, never spaghetti. The rough, porous egg pasta holds the slow-cooked sauce, which simmers for hours. Every family says its own version is the right one.

cards.headline: About this gelateria
cards.note: The porticoes began in the Middle Ages. As the city grew and students needed rooms, buildings extended over the street to make space. Today you can walk the centre in rain or strong sun without an umbrella.

cards.headline: About this salumeria
cards.note: Bologna and Modena have a famous rivalry. In 1325 Modena won the battle of Zappolino and carried off a wooden bucket from a Bolognese well. Modena still keeps it as a symbol today.

cards.headline: About this bookshop
cards.note: Il Gattopardo was written by Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa, a Palermo aristocrat. Publishers turned it down, and it came out in 1958, after his death. Its best-known idea: everything must change so that everything can stay the same.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Here it's arancina, feminine, like the orange (arancia) it's named after. On the other side of Sicily they say arancino and shape it as a cone, like Mount Etna. Both are accepted, but the argument never ends.

cards.headline: About this osteria
cards.note: An osteria was historically a tavern where people came mainly to drink wine. The host, the oste, served a few simple local dishes to go with it. Today many osterie, like this one, serve full meals.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: A full Italian meal runs from antipasto to primo, secondo with contorno, dolce and caffè. Most days people skip courses: at a trattoria many order just a primo, or a secondo with a contorno.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Slow Food began in the 1980s in Bra, a small Piedmont town near Turin. It stands for food that is good, clean and fair: tasty, grown without harming the land, and made by people paid fairly.

cards.headline: About this salumeria
cards.note: A food labelled DOP must come from its own area and be made by set rules. Real Parmigiano Reggiano can only come from a small area including Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena and part of Bologna's province.

cards.note: The Palio is a historic horse race held twice a year in the Campo. Before the race, the horses are blessed.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People feel a deep identity with their neighborhood, their contrada. They mention it with pride, saying Oca or Drago. After a victory, the contrade hold celebration dinners.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Morning coffee is taken standing at the bar.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evening, people go out for the passeggiata along Via di Città. Before dinner, many have an aperitivo, often in Piazza del Campo.

rows.en: a small glass of wine, in Venetian
Shall we go for an ombra?
You buy one at the bacari.
gossip, a chat, in Venetian
Shall we have a little chat?
a small piece, in Venetian
Just a small piece, thanks.
without worries, in Venetian
Go easy, without worries.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Aperitivo hour in Venice means cicchetti and a spritz.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people in Venice do their shopping every day at the Rialto market.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evening, people in Venice go out for a passeggiata, an evening walk, in the campi.

rows.en: Let's go! (in Neapolitan)
Let's go, it's late!
Neapolitan for the Italian andiamo.
Hey! (in Neapolitan)
Hey, how are you?
A casual greeting between friends.
the lad (in Neapolitan)
the girl (in Neapolitan)
That lad is nice.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Caffè sospeso means "suspended coffee". You pay for an extra coffee ahead of time, so that someone in need can have one later.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Via San Gregorio Armeno is where people make presepi, or nativity scenes. The tradition goes on all year round, not just at Christmas.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Sunday pranzo, the big midday meal, is shared with the entire extended family.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people drink their espresso standing at the bar counter, rather than sitting down at a table.

rows.text: La dotta, la grassa, la rossa.
rows.en: The learned, the fat, the red.
La grassa nods to its rich cuisine.
traditional fried bread
One crescentina, please.
Some people call it a tigella.
to take a walk

rows.text: Facciamo quattro passi sotto i portici?
rows.en: Shall we walk under the porticoes?
Literally, 'to make four steps'.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Coffee is drunk standing at the bar, not sitting down.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Aperitivo hour is a custom here, with wine and mortadella.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Making fresh pasta by hand is an art. The sfoglina rolls out the dough, which is called "tirare la sfoglia".

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People take real pride in having the oldest university in the Western world.

rows.en: let's go, in Sicilian
Let's go, it's late!
come in, in Sicilian
Come in, come in!
good heavens!, in Sicilian
Good heavens, it's late!

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evening, many people take a passeggiata in the piazzas. It is a slow stroll, part of the daily rhythm.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people have their morning coffee standing at the bar. Coffee is a ritual that comes back through the day.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Street food is eaten while walking. It is part of how people eat out and about.

rows.en: sir, in Milanese
Good morning, sir!
madam, in Milanese
Good evening, madam!
work, in Milanese
I have a lot of work today.
hey
Hey, how's it going?

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The aperitivo hour starts at 6pm. On Sundays the aperitivo is a ritual of its own.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Cappuccino is always only a morning drink. For a quick espresso, people stand at the bar.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Fashion week comes twice a year. The Salone del Mobile, the furniture fair, takes place in April.

rows.en: hello, in Bergamasco
People use it as a greeting.
still, in Bergamasco
It is the local way to say ancora.
up high, in Bergamasco
down low, in Bergamasco
Locals use the pair to tell high from low.
the upper city, in Bergamasco
It is the dialect name for the upper city.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evening people go out for a passeggiata along Il Sentierone. It is a favorite place for a slow walk.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Aperitivo time is around 7pm. Many people have it with local wines.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Sant'Alessandro is the patron saint, and he is celebrated every year on August 26.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The traditional Sunday pranzo is a big meal with the extended family.

rows.en: Don't move!, in Piedmontese
A common local expression.
slice, in Piedmontese
Used for bread or cake.
snack, in Piedmontese
traditional afternoon snack meal

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Taking the ritual bicerin is a local custom. It is a drink made of coffee, chocolate and cream.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Aperitivo hour here comes with the local vermouth and an abundant buffet.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Coffee is taken standing at the bar, never sitting down.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Shopping under the elegant arcades, the portici, is a favourite local custom.

rows.en: ugh, a sigh of annoyance
Ugh, it's so hot!
A common exclamation you hear often.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Aperitivo in Piazza delle Erbe is a local custom. An aperitivo is a drink with small bites before dinner, taken with friends in the square.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The town is flat, so the bicycle is essential for getting around. Locals cycle everywhere.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Torta sbrisolona is a local cake, crumbly and sweet. It is often eaten with coffee.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Locals like an evening stroll in Piazza Sordello. In Italian, a stroll like this is called a passeggiata.

rows.en: to be capable
Lucia is very capable.
You say it about someone who is good at what they do.
what?, in Tuscan
What do you want?
A traditional Tuscan way to say "cosa?"
dad

rows.text: Il mio babbo è a casa.
rows.en: My dad is at home.
People here say "babbo" instead of "papà".
little boy, child
The little boy plays in the square.
People here call children "bimbo".

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: A favourite evening custom is the passeggiata, a walk along the city walls. People also cycle on top of the Renaissance walls.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Aperitivo hour is a local custom, and Piazza San Michele is one of the places where people enjoy it.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On Saturday mornings people go shopping at the Mercato del Carmine.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On Sundays you can hear concerts in the city's historic churches.

rows.en: if only, I wish
Coming with us? If only!
I wish I had more time.
slowly, carefully
Drive slowly, carefully, please.
Walk carefully on the stones.
a little drop (of wine)
A little drop of wine?
Yes, just a little drop.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Wine tasting in the tufa caves is a local custom. The caves are cool, which is why people say al fresco, "in the cool", about them.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Life here is split between the town up on the cliff and the land below it. Many people take the funicolare up to the town from the train station.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In autumn, people go truffle hunting in the woods nearby. Truffle then appears in local dishes, such as umbrichelli al tartufo and bruschetta al tartufo nero.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Before dinner, people gather in the piazza for an aperitivo. It's a relaxed way to see friends and ease into the evening.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Visitors and locals go to see the Pozzo di San Patrizio, a well, for good luck.

rows.en: let's go, in Sicilian
Let's go, it's late!
It can also mean "move it".
boy, in Sicilian
girl, in Sicilian
What beauty!, in Sicilian
What beauty, the sea!
buon appetito, in Sicilian
Enjoy your meal, everyone!

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In summer, breakfast here can be granita with a brioche. It is a local custom for the warm months.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In December there are celebrations for Santa Lucia. They are one of the customs people keep here.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Every year at Pentecost, at the end of the morning Mass, Rome's firefighters drop thousands of red rose petals through the oculus. They stand for the Holy Spirit coming down.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The long oval of Piazza Navona follows the shape of the Stadium of Domitian that once stood here. At its centre is Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Il Gesù, the mother church of the Jesuits, holds the tomb of Saint Ignatius of Loyola. Baciccio's ceiling fresco from the late 1600s seems to spill into the nave. Entry is free.

cards.headline: About this osteria
cards.note: In Roman cooking, gricia is guanciale and pecorino. Add tomato and it is amatriciana; add egg yolks instead and it is carbonara, never cream.

cards.headline: About this station
cards.note: Stazione Termini takes its name from the nearby Baths of Diocletian, the terme.

cards.headline: About this deli
cards.note: Testaccio grew around Rome's slaughterhouse. The cuts its workers took home, the quinto quarto, became Roman classics: coda alla vaccinara, trippa and pajata.

cards.headline: About this kiosk
cards.note: Grattachecca is ice shaved by hand from a block into a glass, then covered with syrup: tamarind, mint, lemon or amarena, with fresh fruit. Romans argue about the best flavour.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Santa Maria in Trastevere is one of Rome's oldest churches, with an apse covered in medieval gold mosaics. Near the altar, fons olei marks where a spring of oil is said to have flowed.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: This bar is carved into the tufa of the Sassi. People drink their coffee standing at the counter, quick and strong, then look out over the ravine from the outside tables.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Peperoni cruschi are dried peppers fried until crisp. Wild greens like cime di rapa are sold here too, and they go into orecchiette.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Pane di Matera is made with durum wheat semolina and has its own IGP label. On the menu it sits beside crapiata, a soup of grains and pulses.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This cave house in the Sassi is kept as a family lived in it, with the bed, the loom and the corner for the animals.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The cathedral is dedicated to the Madonna della Bruna, patron saint of the city. On her festa, 2 July, a decorated papier-mâché carriage is pulled through the streets, and at the end the crowd tears it apart.

cards.headline: About this workshop
cards.note: The cucù is a little clay whistle shaped like a rooster. It is a symbol of the city and a gift for good luck.

cards.headline: About this bridge
cards.note: The Ponte Vecchio is known as the bridge of the goldsmiths. Some of its tiny family workshops make and repair jewellery.

cards.headline: About this loggia
cards.note: The Loggia dei Lanzi is an open arcade of statues, free to walk into. Cellini's bronze Perseus, holding up Medusa's head, has stood at the front since 1554.

cards.headline: About this coffee bar
cards.note: Some bars here brought speciality coffee: single-origin beans, roasted lighter, made slowly as an espresso or a filter coffee. It tastes quite different from the usual bar coffee.

cards.headline: About this street-food stall
cards.note: Lampredotto is a bread roll filled with the slow-cooked fourth stomach of the cow, dipped in its broth and topped with green sauce. For locals it's real street food.

cards.headline: About this trattoria
cards.note: At this lunch-only trattoria, strangers share tables. The menu includes ribollita, trippa alla fiorentina, and bistecca alla fiorentina, served rare or not at all.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Every June, the Calcio Storico, the rough old football game, is played on sand in Piazza Santa Croce. A statue of Dante stands in the square.

cards.headline: About this bakery
cards.note: Ricciarelli are soft almond biscuits dusted with icing sugar. Panforte is a dense cake of candied fruit, nuts and spices. Both are local Christmas sweets with medieval roots.

cards.headline: About this osteria
cards.note: Pici are thick hand-rolled spaghetti made of flour and water, with no egg. They are dressed with cacio e pepe or with aglione, a big garlic from the Val di Chiana.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The square is shell-shaped, with its paving divided into nine sections. The Palazzo Pubblico stands at the bottom of the slope, under the Torre del Mangia.

cards.headline: About this shop
cards.note: The Palio's prize is the drappellone, a banner painted anew by a different artist for each race. Each contrada has its own colors and emblem, such as the Eagle or the Snail.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Seasonal stalls sell what local dishes call for: cavolo nero for ribollita, beans for fagioli all'uccelletto, and tomatoes to go with stale pane toscano in a panzanella.

cards.headline: About this square
cards.note: This quiet square lies in front of Palazzo Salimbeni, the seat of the Monte dei Paschi bank. It is among the oldest banks in the world.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Open since 1720 under the arcades of Piazza San Marco. A coffee at a table costs far more than at the bar, and when the orchestra plays, a music charge is added.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Moleche are lagoon crabs caught just as they shed their shell, and only in certain seasons. Locals come here early for them, and for sardines and cuttlefish.

cards.headline: About this crossing
cards.note: The traghetto is a plain gondola with no seats, rowed by two gondoliers across the Grand Canal. Made for Venetians crossing with shopping, it costs two euros, or seventy cents with a Venezia Unica card.

cards.headline: About this square
cards.note: Statues of merchants in oriental dress line the walls, said to be the Mastelli brothers from the Morea. One, Sior Rioba, has an iron nose and counts among the city's "talking statues".

cards.headline: About this boatyard
cards.note: It is one of the few boatyards still building and repairing gondolas by hand, from several kinds of wood. The yard looks like a mountain chalet on the canal.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Caffè Gambrinus is a grand belle époque café on Piazza Trieste e Trento, open since 1860. It stands steps from the Teatro San Carlo and Palazzo Reale, and writers and artists have long met here.

cards.headline: About this station
cards.note: At Napoli Centrale the fast trains to Rome and Salerno arrive. The Circumvesuviana to Pompei and Sorrento leaves from the level below. It is run by a separate company, EAV, with its own tickets.

cards.headline: About this mozzarella shop
cards.note: Mozzarella di bufala campana is a protected product, made from buffalo milk. It is sold in its own whey and is best when very fresh.

cards.headline: About this street-food window
cards.note: Pizza a portafoglio is a small margherita or marinara folded in four like a wallet and wrapped in paper. It is eaten walking, for a couple of euros.

cards.headline: About this street
cards.note: Spaccanapoli is the long straight street that cuts the old city in two. It follows the old Greek and Roman grid of Naples.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Bolognese call this group of linked churches Sette Chiese, the seven churches, though fewer remain today. Its oldest parts are over a thousand years old, and anyone can walk in freely.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This portico runs almost four kilometres under 666 arches, up the hill to a sanctuary. It is the longest in the world, and the city's porticoes became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

cards.headline: About this salumeria
cards.note: The Quadrilatero, the old market streets off Piazza Maggiore, has had food stalls since the Middle Ages. Mortadella is sold sliced to order by weight, and Parmigiano Reggiano by age: 24 or 36 months.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The two towers, the Asinelli and the leaning Garisenda, were built in the 1100s. Back then the city bristled with towers.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This building from the 1500s was the seat of the city's university, the oldest in Europe. Its walls are covered in the coats of arms of its old students.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: In Palermo, brioche col gelato is a classic, eaten at the bar or on the go. The brioche is the soft round one with a little "tuppo" on top.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The giant old Ficus magnolioides trees here were brought from Australia in the 19th century. Their aerial roots hang down and spread into trunks, like a cave.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Palermitans call this great marble fountain the Fontana della Vergogna, the fountain of shame, because of its nude statues.

cards.headline: About this crossroads
cards.note: This baroque crossroads sits at the heart of the old city. Its four corner facades show the four seasons, four Spanish kings and four of the city's patron saints.

cards.headline: About this chapel
cards.note: This was the royal chapel of Palermo's Norman kings. Gold Byzantine mosaics shine under a painted wooden ceiling made by Arab craftsmen.

cards.headline: About this street-food stall
cards.note: At Ballarò market, pani ca' meusa sellers ask "schietta o maritata?": plain, with lemon, or "married", with ricotta and caciocavallo.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: At six the bar fills for aperitivo, the Milanese way: a drink with something to eat. The Negroni sbagliato was invented in Milan, with sparkling wine where the gin should be.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Gorgonzola is named after a town just east of Milan. Taleggio is a soft square cheese from Val Taleggio in the Bergamo Alps. Salame milano is a mild, finely ground salami.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: The Veneranda Fabbrica has looked after the Duomo since 1387. Its restorers have been at work on the cathedral ever since.

cards.headline: About this arcade
cards.note: The Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II is an arcade of iron and glass. Milanesi call it il salotto, the city's living room.

cards.headline: About this trattoria
cards.note: An old Milanese trattoria serves risotto alla milanese, made with saffron, alongside cotoletta and ossobuco. In winter there is also cassoeula.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: The Campanone, the Torre Civica on Piazza Vecchia, still rings one hundred strokes every night at ten. It once signalled the closing of the city gates.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Polenta e osei is the town's sweet. It's a dessert shaped like a small mound of polenta, with a little bird on top.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Casoncelli are a Bergamo classic: filled pasta served with butter, sage and pancetta.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Cappella Colleoni is the chapel the condottiero Bartolomeo Colleoni built for his own tomb. Inside, you can see paintings by Tiepolo.

cards.headline: About this funicular
cards.note: This funicular has carried people between the lower town and Bergamo Alta since 1887. It climbs up through the Venetian walls.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: Caffè San Carlo sits on Piazza San Carlo, the square Turinese call their "salotto," or drawing room. Inside, with gilded mirrors and chandeliers, most people drink their coffee standing at the bar.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: Al Bicerin has served the bicerin since 1763. The drink is coffee, chocolate and cream in separate layers, never stirred. "Bicerin" is Piedmontese for "small glass," which is what it comes in.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Porta Palazzo is one of the biggest open-air markets in Europe. Turinese shop here for the peppers, cardoons and herbs behind dishes like bagna cauda and acciughe al verde.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Del Cambio has been open since 1757, across from Palazzo Carignano. Cavour had his own table here. It's a place for Piedmont's classics: agnolotti del plin, vitello tonnato and bunet.

cards.headline: About this shop
cards.note: Vermouth di Torino is a wine flavoured with herbs and spices. Turin made it famous, and it is the heart of the aperitivo hour.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Mole Antonelliana is the tower that is the symbol of Turin. Inside it is the Museo Nazionale del Cinema, the national cinema museum.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Sbrisolona, the crumbly almond cake of the area, is broken by hand, not cut. It often comes with a coffee or a sweet wine.

cards.headline: About this deli
cards.note: Salame mantovano, grana padano and mostarda mantovana are what people from here want on the table. In winter, cotechino joins them.

cards.headline: About this palace
cards.note: This is the Gonzaga palace, with hundreds of rooms. It's where Mantegna painted the Camera degli Sposi.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The square lies in front of the Palazzo Ducale and the cathedral. Music has deep roots here: Claudio Monteverdi worked at the Gonzaga court in this town.

cards.headline: About this station
cards.note: The city is flat and bordered by three lakes. The old centre is only a short walk from the station.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: This historic café on Via Fillungo has been open since 1846 and is loved for its Art Nouveau interior. Try the buccellato, Lucca's sweet bread with raisins and anise.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Local salumi like prosciutto bazzone and biroldo are sold here. The sellers let you taste before you buy, so you can try something new without any worry.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Duomo di San Martino keeps the Volto Santo, a wooden crucifix. Every 13 September, Lucca carries it through the streets.

cards.headline: About this tower
cards.note: The Torre Guinigi is a medieval tower with holm oaks growing on its roof. Trees at the top of a tower are a surprising sight.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Piazza Anfiteatro is an oval square built on the walls of a Roman amphitheatre. Tourists and locals sit at its cafés, and the crowd is even bigger on antique-market days.

cards.headline: About this well
cards.note: This deep well was dug for a pope in the 1500s. It has two spiral staircases that never meet.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: The Duomo has a golden façade on the square. Inside, the Cappella di San Brizio holds Signorelli's frescoes of the end of the world.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: This restaurant is carved into the tufa under the town. It serves Umbrian food: umbrichelli, a thick hand-rolled pasta, plus wild boar and porchetta.

cards.headline: About this station
cards.note: The old town stands on a tall block of volcanic tuff. The funicolare climbs from beside the station to Piazza Cahen, at the edge of the old town.

cards.headline: About this shop
cards.note: The town has made pottery since the Middle Ages. In workshops like this one, near the Duomo, ceramics are still painted by hand, and visitors can see how it is done.

cards.headline: About this bar
cards.note: In Ortigia, people stop at the corner bar for espresso at the marble counter. In summer, the classic Siracusa breakfast is granita with a soft brioche.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Siracusans come early to the Ortigia morning market for fresh fish like swordfish and tuna. Stalls also sell blood oranges, Siracusa lemons and capers, and sellers shout their prices over the crowd.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Fonte Aretusa is a freshwater spring right by the sea, where papyrus grows. It is named after the nymph of the Greek legend.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The Parco Archeologico della Neapolis has a Greek theatre cut into the rock. The park also has a cave called the Ear of Dionysius.

cards.headline: About this cultural site
cards.note: The Giudecca is Ortigia's old Jewish quarter, with narrow streets. A Jewish ritual bath was found deep under a palazzo there.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Pantheon was a Roman temple, rebuilt under Hadrian in the 100s AD. Its dome has an open circle at the top, the oculus, and it is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Il Gesù is the mother church of the Jesuits, built in the late 1500s. St Ignatius of Loyola, who founded the order, is buried here, and its style influenced many Baroque churches.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: Villa Borghese began as the gardens of Cardinal Scipione Borghese in the early 1600s. Today it is one of Rome's largest public parks, and it holds the Galleria Borghese, an art museum.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Piazza Navona follows the shape of an ancient Roman stadium built by Domitian, which is why it is so long and narrow. In the middle stands Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: This square is the heart of Trastevere, with a fountain in the middle and the basilica's mosaic façade along one side. It is a favorite place to meet and spend the evening.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Santa Maria in Trastevere is one of the oldest churches in Rome dedicated to Mary, first founded in the 200s. The shining gold mosaics inside date mostly from the 1100s and 1200s.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Colosseum opened in AD 80 and could hold about 50,000 people. Crowds came to watch gladiator fights and other shows. Its official name was the Flavian Amphitheatre.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This cave home is furnished as families once lived in it. One room often held the beds, the tools and the animals together. People lived in the Sassi this way until the 1950s.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: Across the ravine from the Sassi, this park protects wild plateau land and many rock-hewn churches, some with faded frescoes inside. Hermit monks once lived and prayed in these caves.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Under this square lies the Palombaro Lungo, a huge cistern built in the 1800s to store rainwater. It was forgotten for decades and is now open to visitors.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The cathedral on this square is Romanesque, finished in 1270. Each July, a decorated cart for the Madonna della Bruna is paraded through town, then torn apart by the crowd.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Ponte Vecchio has carried shops since the Middle Ages. Butchers once worked here, but in the 1500s the Medici replaced them with goldsmiths and jewellers, who are still there today.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The Boboli Gardens stretch behind Palazzo Pitti, once the home of the Medici family. Laid out in the 1500s, they became a model for formal gardens at other European courts.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Palazzo Vecchio, Florence's town hall, overlooks this square. In 1498 the preacher Savonarola was burned here, and a round plaque in the paving marks the spot.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Brunelleschi designed Santo Spirito, but it was built after his death. Its plain front was never decorated, so the church looks smooth and bare from the square.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Every June the square is covered in sand for calcio storico, a rough old form of football. Teams from Florence's historic quarters play it, and the final falls on 24 June.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: Cascine comes from the word for farmhouses and dairy farms. The land was a Medici estate for farming and hunting, and it later became a public park along the Arno.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The Campo slopes down like a shell toward the town hall. Twice each summer, the Palio horse race is run around its edge: bareback riders, three fast laps.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The grand Palazzo Salimbeni is the headquarters of Monte dei Paschi, a bank founded in 1472. It is counted among the oldest banks in the world.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The tower beside the town hall is named after its first bell ringer, nicknamed Mangiaguadagni, meaning roughly "profit-eater". Built in the 1300s, it rises over 80 metres.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Rialto has been the center of Venetian trade since the Middle Ages. Fish, fruit and vegetables are still sold here in the morning, and the fish market sits in a neo-Gothic building from 1907.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The stone Rialto Bridge was finished in 1591, replacing older wooden bridges. Until 1854 it was the only way to cross the Grand Canal on foot.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Campo Santa Margherita is one of the largest squares in Venice. It's lively with students from the nearby university of Ca' Foscari, and its cafés and bars fill up in the evening.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Statues of men in turbans stand on the walls here. They are said to be merchants from the Morea, the Mastelli brothers, and the painter Tintoretto lived close by.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: One of Naples' oldest street markets, it runs through the old city. Stalls sell fresh fish, fruit, vegetables and street food, and the vendors call out their prices.

cards.headline: About this castle
cards.note: This is the oldest standing castle in Naples, built on a small islet. Legend says the poet Virgil hid an egg in its foundations; if it breaks, disaster follows.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: King Ferdinand I gave this estate to his wife, Lucia Migliaccio, Duchess of Floridia, in the early 1800s. From its gardens you look out over the Bay of Naples.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Two medieval towers, Asinelli and Garisenda, lean over the city centre. Asinelli is about 97 metres tall and can be climbed. The shorter Garisenda leans so much that Dante mentioned it.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Santo Stefano is not one church but a group of linked churches and courtyards, known as the Sette Chiese, the seven churches. It was built to recall the holy places of Jerusalem.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: This is Bologna's main square, with the huge basilica of San Petronio on one side. On summer evenings it becomes an open-air cinema, with films shown on a big screen.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This covered walkway is the longest portico in the world, about 3.8 kilometres and nearly 700 arches. It climbs the hill from the city to the sanctuary of the Madonna di San Luca.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Archiginnasio was the main building of the University of Bologna. Its walls and ceilings are covered with the painted coats of arms of students, and inside is a carved wooden anatomical theatre.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Ballarò is one of Palermo's oldest street markets, with roots in the Arab period. Its name is thought to come from Balhara, a village near Monreale. Stalls sell fruit, fish and street food.

cards.headline: About this theatre
cards.note: Teatro Massimo is the largest opera house in Italy and one of the largest in Europe. It opened in 1897. Its steps appear in the final scene of The Godfather Part III.

cards.headline: About this garden
cards.note: The giant fig trees here came from Australia in the 1800s. Their roots hang down from the branches and grow into new trunks.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The fountain here was made in Florence in the 1500s for a private villa, then bought by Palermo. Its many nude statues led locals to call it the Fountain of Shame.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Quattro Canti stands where two main streets cross, dividing the old centre into four districts. Its four Baroque facades each have a fountain, statues of a season, a Spanish king and a patron saint.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: Work on Milan's cathedral began in 1386 and went on for almost six hundred years. Its marble roof is covered in spires and statues, and visitors can walk up onto it.

cards.headline: About this arcade
cards.note: This glass-roofed arcade opened in 1877 and joins the Duomo's square to the one by La Scala opera house. On the floor, people spin on their heel on the mosaic bull for good luck.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Beside the piazza stands the Torre Civica, called the Campanone. Every evening at 10 it rings 100 strokes, a custom that goes back to when the city gates were closed for the night.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This chapel was built in the 1470s as the tomb of Bartolomeo Colleoni, a famous mercenary captain. Its richly patterned marble front is a Renaissance showpiece, and Colleoni is buried inside.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Built in the late 1700s as the Teatro Riccardi, this theatre was renamed in 1897 for Gaetano Donizetti, the opera composer born in Bergamo in 1797.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Porta Palazzo is among the largest open-air markets in Europe. Its stalls fill Piazza della Repubblica with fruit, vegetables, cheese, fish and much more.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Mole was begun in the 1860s as a synagogue. Today it houses the National Cinema Museum, and its tall spire is the symbol of Turin. It appears on the Italian 2-cent euro coin.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The park runs along the Po river. Inside is the Borgo Medievale, a village built in 1884 as a copy of medieval Piedmont, plus the Castello del Valentino, a former Savoy residence.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Palazzo Madama stands in the middle of the square. Its oldest part is a Roman gate. It later became a castle, then the first seat of the Senate of unified Italy.

cards.headline: About this palace
cards.note: This was the home of the Gonzaga family, who ruled Mantua for centuries. It is a huge complex of palaces and courtyards. Inside, the Camera degli Sposi has frescoes by Andrea Mantegna.

cards.headline: About this palace
cards.note: Giulio Romano built this villa in the 1520s and 1530s for Federico II Gonzaga, as a retreat just outside the city. Its Sala dei Giganti is painted with falling giants on walls and ceiling.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: Mantua's grand medieval square has the cathedral and Palazzo Ducale on its sides. The Bonacolsi family ruled from here until the Gonzaga seized power in 1328.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The cathedral holds the Volto Santo, a wooden crucifix that Lucca has honored since the Middle Ages. Each September a candlelit procession celebrates it.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Oak trees grow in a small rooftop garden at the top of this brick tower. You can climb the stairs for a view over the rooftops of Lucca.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: Lucca's botanical garden was founded in 1820 by Maria Luisa of Bourbon, who then ruled Lucca. It is a quiet green space with a pond.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: This oval piazza follows the shape of a Roman amphitheatre. Over the centuries houses were built into its walls, and the arena became the square you see today.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The church here, San Michele in Foro, stands on the site of the Roman forum. A statue of the archangel Michael stands on top of its decorated façade.

cards.headline: About this cathedral
cards.note: Construction began in 1290 to honour the Miracle of Bolsena, when a host was said to bleed onto a linen cloth. That cloth, the corporal, is still kept in the cathedral.

cards.headline: About this well
cards.note: Pope Clement VII ordered this well after the 1527 Sack of Rome, fearing a siege. Two separate spiral staircases let donkeys carrying water go down and come up without meeting.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: Ortigia's open-air market sits beside the ruins of the ancient Temple of Apollo. In the mornings, stalls sell fresh fish, fruit, vegetables and cheese, and some also serve street food made on the spot.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: In Greek myth, the nymph Arethusa escaped the river god Alpheus by turning into this spring. Fresh water still wells up just steps from the sea, in a pool filled with papyrus plants.

cards.headline: About this park
cards.note: The park holds an ancient Greek theatre cut straight into the rock of the hillside. Classical plays are still performed there every late spring, as they were over two thousand years ago.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The piazza is named for Archimedes, the great mathematician born in ancient Syracuse. At its center stands the Fountain of Diana, where the goddess is surrounded by sea creatures.

rows.en: Walking into a shop. What time is it?
Good morning. Until early afternoon.
Good evening. From mid-afternoon on.

cards.headline: This or that: friend or stranger

rows.en: Asking how someone is: friend or stranger?
How are you? To a friend or child.
How are you? To a stranger or shopkeeper.
Getting someone's attention: friend or stranger?
Excuse me! To a friend.
Excuse me! To a stranger or official.

cards.headline: This or that: do you like it?

rows.en: Asking if someone likes it: friend or stranger?
Do you like it? To a friend.
Do you like it? To someone you call Lei.
A friend says they like coffee.
Me too. You like it as well.
Not me. You don't like it.

cards.headline: This or that: I'll take it

rows.en: Deciding to buy something. Which word fits?
I'll take it. A masculine thing, like il pane.
I'll take it. A feminine thing, like la pasta.

cards.headline: This or that: where is it?

rows.en: Asking where something is: one thing or several?
Where's the pharmacy? One thing.
Where are the peaches? Several things.

cards.headline: This or that: telling the time

rows.en: What time is it?
It's three o'clock.
It's one o'clock.

cards.headline: This or that: how you travel

rows.en: How are you getting here?
I come by train.
I come on foot.

cards.headline: This or that: at what time

rows.en: At what time?
At three o'clock.
At noon.
How much would you like?
A kilo of tomatoes, for a big shop.
Half a kilo of tomatoes, for a smaller one.
Asking for some bread at the counter.
I'd like a bit of bread.
I'd like some bread.

cards.headline: This or that: this one or that one

rows.en: This one or that one?
This one, thanks. It's close to you.
That one over there, please.
Asking where someone's from: man or woman?
Are you American? Asking a man.
Are you American? Asking a woman.
Whose is it?
It's mine. A masculine thing.
It's mine. A feminine thing.
Asking the waiter for the bill.
Could you bring me the bill? Just me.
Could you bring us the bill? For the table.

cards.headline: This or that: right or left

rows.en: Right or left?
To the right.
To the left.

Siracusa: they say arancino.

Palermo: you eat the arancina.
